run_detail.final_report_markdown:
# JSON Indexing in MySQL 8.4 and PostgreSQL 17: A Comparative Synthesis MySQL 8.4 and PostgreSQL 17 both provide dedicated indexing facilities for JSON data, but the frozen evidence describes different mechanisms: MySQL optimizes queries on JSON columns of InnoDB tables that use JSON_OVERLAPS() in the WHERE clause via multi-valued indexes, while PostgreSQL provides GIN index operator classes whose supported operators and performance characteristics vary. The available evidence does not establish a full side-by-side coverage of JSON index types, accelerated operators, or index cost; it instead supports several specific claims about each system. ## JSON Indexing in MySQL 8.4 In MySQL 8.4, the documented optimization path for JSON columns in InnoDB tables begins with the WHERE clause. Queries that use JSON_OVERLAPS() against a JSON column can be optimized by multi-valued indexes. This is stated repeatedly in the frozen evidence, confirming that the optimizer recognizes that specific function-based predicate as eligible for multi-valued index access rather than requiring a full scan of the JSON column. [evidence:631155c91f66a29dd9f08746b6f3e56d48cd37f1a2a10955] [evidence:85dafc57487b4eddb579388cdc38aa9d86dc2da78d19e4a5] On the maintenance side, multi-valued indexes in MySQL behave like ordinary indexes with respect to data manipulation. DML operations that affect a multi-valued index are processed in the same manner as DML affecting a normal index, and the only difference is that a single clustered index record may generate more than one insert or update for the multi-valued index. This means the presence of multi-valued indexes does not introduce a separate DML path; it simply changes the number of index entries that a single row operation can produce. [evidence:e4ccdc75dbc9e75339720517de703c1f033d66bb509485d3] ## JSON Indexing in PostgreSQL 17 PostgreSQL 17 offers GIN indexes for JSON data, and among the supported operator classes is jsonb_path_ops. That operator class supports the @> containment operator as well as the @? and @@ operators, which perform jsonpath matching. This gives users a targeted index type for queries expressed as containment or jsonpath predicates rather than requiring a general-purpose index to cover every JSON query shape. [evidence:6e05f8b2e49fe6dbd54724f86264e0ceed6ba310820ca74d] The jsonb_path_ops operator class is also described in terms of index cost. It is usually much smaller than a jsonb_ops index built over the same data, and its search specificity is better, especially when queries contain keys that appear frequently in the data. Although it supports only the @>, @?, and @@ operators, it has notable performance advantages over the default jsonb_ops operator class. Together, these statements indicate that the narrower operator coverage of jsonb_path_ops is accompanied by reduced index size and improved search specificity. [evidence:0f2d6e7a660f8d1d9355af9580ef31ec892fbe1643fb2cf9] [evidence:7850d23cf30c549f4b8d2586b1a0aaaf6fb4c9b2219914d2] [evidence:d97b6238b6a99e7af23c8efc38da9557034f8c783c0f5845] ## 对比表 | System | JSON index type / operator class | Operators or predicates that can be accelerated | Index cost characteristics | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | MySQL 8.4 | Multi-valued indexes on JSON columns of InnoDB tables | JSON_OVERLAPS() in the WHERE clause | Not specified in frozen evidence for multi-valued indexes; DML handling is the same as a normal index, except that a single clustered index record may require more than one insert or update. [evidence:631155c91f66a29dd9f08746b6f3e56d48cd37f1a2a10955] [evidence:85dafc57487b4eddb579388cdc38aa9d86dc2da78d19e4a5] [evidence:e4ccdc75dbc9e75339720517de703c1f033d66bb509485d3] | | PostgreSQL 17 | jsonb_path_ops GIN operator class | @>, @?, @@ | Usually much smaller than a jsonb_ops index over the same data; search specificity is better, particularly when queries contain frequently occurring keys; notable performance advantages over jsonb_ops. Queries on JSON columns of `InnoDB` tables using `JSON_OVERLAPS()` in the
`WHERE` clause can be optimized using
multi-valued indexes.

DML operations that affect multi-valued indexes are handled
in the same way as DML operations that affect a normal
index, with the only difference being that there may be more
than one insert or update for a single clustered index
record.
Although the `jsonb_path_ops` operator class supports only queries with the `@>`, `@?` and `@@` operators, it has notable performance advantages over the default operator class `jsonb_ops`.
GIN indexes also support the `@?` and `@@` operators, which perform `jsonpath` matching.

A `jsonb_path_ops` index is usually much smaller than a `jsonb_ops` index over the same data, and the specificity of searches is better, particularly when queries contain keys that appear frequently in the data.

data.candidate_value: A `jsonb_path_ops` index is usually much smaller than a `jsonb_ops` index over the same data, and the specificity of searches is better, particularly when queries contain keys that appear frequently in the data.

data.candidate_value: Although the `jsonb_path_ops` operator class supports only queries with the `@>`, `@?` and `@@` operators, it has notable performance advantages over the default operator class `jsonb_ops`.

equivalent_claims.claim_text: Although the `jsonb_path_ops` operator class supports only queries with the `@>`, `@?` and `@@` operators, it has notable performance advantages over the default operator class `jsonb_ops`.
Of the two operator classes for type `jsonb`, `jsonb_ops` is the default. `jsonb_path_ops` supports fewer operators but offers better performance for those operators.
